Indonesia has a Mixed public-private (BPJS Kesehatan for residents) healthcare system, rated moderate quality. Typical costs for tourists: System: Mixed public-private (BPJS Kesehatan for residents) Quality: ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Healthcare quality varies significantly. Bali has good private international clinics and hospitals with English-speaking staff (BIMC, Sanglah public hospital). Java (Jakarta) has excellent international hospitals. Rural islands have very limited healthcare. Medical evacuation to Singapore or Australia may be necessary for serious conditions. 💡 Medical Tourism Indonesia is not typically a medical tourism destination for Westerners — rather, locals sometimes travel OUT for medical care. Bali does attract 'wellness tourists' for spa, yoga, and detox retreats.. Pharmacy access: easy. Access: easy Hours: Pharmacies (apotek) are common in Bali and major cities, typically open 9am-9pm. Some 24/7 pharmacies exist in larger cities. In smaller islands, pharmacy access is limited. Prescription rules: Many medications available OTC. For prescription medications, a local doctor's prescription may be required. International prescriptions are generally not accepted. Counterfeit medications are a real risk — use reputable pharmacies. 💡 Tips Many common medications are available without prescription, including antibiotics. However, quality can be inconsistent and counterfeit medications are a concern. Buy from reputable pharmacies (Kimia Farma, Guardian, or international clinics) when possible. Bring all prescription medications you may need. Recommended vaccinations: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (for rural Java/Bali), Rabies (for animal contact — Bali has rabies), COVID-19 (following current guidelines). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: ⚠️ Strongly recommended Average cost: $25-50/week 💡 Tip Medical evacuation from Bali to Singapore (3-4 hours) or Australia is often necessary for serious conditions. Ensure your insurance covers emergency evacuation. International clinics in Bali (especially in Seminyak, Ubud, Sanur) have direct billing with major insurers. 💡 Tip Medical evacuation from Bali to Singapore (3-4 hours) or Australia is often necessary for serious conditions. Thailand has an overall safety risk rated as low. Violent crime is low and petty crime (pickpocketing, scams) is moderate. The US State Department advises: Exercise Increased Caution. Exercise increased caution in Thailand due to risk of unrest. Some areas have increased risk. Violent crime is rare against tourists but does occur. For solo female travelers: Generally safe. Exercise normal caution at night, especially on islands and in nightlife areas. Drink spiking occurs — watch your drinks. Full moon parties on Koh Phangan require extra vigilance.. LGBTQ+ safety: Very tolerant culturally. Thailand is one of the most LGBTQ+-friendly countries in Asia. Same-sex marriage legalized in 2024. Bangkok has a vibrant LGBTQ+ scene. Kathoey (transgender women) are culturally visible.. Natural disaster risks include: flooding (monsoon season), tsunamis (Andaman coast), earthquakes (northern region).

In Thailand, call 191 for police, 1669 for ambulance/medical emergency, and 199 for fire services. Tourist police: 1155 (English-speaking, available 24/7). This should be your first call for non-emergency issues. The U.S. Embassy Bangkok in Bangkok can be reached at +66-2-205-4000.

Thailand has a Mixed public/private healthcare system, rated good quality. Typical costs for tourists: Private hospitals cater to medical tourists and are excellent quality. Clinic visit $30-80. Emergency room $100-500. Private hospital stay $150-500/night. Bumrungrad International Hospital (Bangkok) is world-class. Public hospitals are cheaper ($10-50) but crowded with long waits and limited English.. Pharmacy access: Pharmacies are everywhere and many medications available OTC that require prescriptions in Western countries — including some antibiotics and pain medications. Pharmacists often speak basic English.. Bangkok has world-class private hospitals (Bumrungrad, Bangkok Hospital, Samitivej) popular with medical tourists. Outside Bangkok, quality drops significantly. Chiang Mai has adequate private hospitals. Islands and rural areas have very limited medical facilities — serious cases require evacuation to Bangkok. Recommended vaccinations: Routine, Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (if rural), Rabies (if rural/animal contact). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Travel insurance advice: Travel insurance essential. Private hospitals require proof of insurance or cash deposit upfront ($500-2,000). Medevac coverage strongly recommended if visiting islands or rural areas.
Adderall / amphetamines is banned in Thailand. Strictly illegal. Thailand has severe drug penalties including long prison sentences. No exemption for foreign prescriptions.
CBD / cannabis products is restricted in Thailand. Cannabis was re-criminalized in 2025. CBD products with >0.2% THC are illegal. Enforcement is increasing. Do not bring any cannabis products.
Codeine is restricted in Thailand. Controlled substance. Bring prescription documentation and keep in original packaging. Maximum 30 days supply.
Tramadol is restricted in Thailand. Classified as a narcotic. Bring doctor's letter and original prescription. Keep in original packaging.
Benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium) is restricted in Thailand. Psychotropic substances requiring documentation. Carry original prescription and doctor's letter. Max 30-day supply.

Typical costs for tourists: System: Mixed public-private (Social Health Insurance for residents) Quality: ★★★☆☆ (3/5) Healthcare varies dramatically between major cities and rural areas. Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City have good private international clinics and hospitals with English-speaking staff. Public hospitals are overcrowded and often lack English. Private healthcare is affordable by Western standards. 💡 Medical Tourism Vietnam is developing as a a medical tourism destination, particularly for dental work and cosmetic surgery, at significantly lower costs than Western countries.. Pharmacy access: very_easy. Access: very_easy Hours: Pharmacies (nhà thuốc) are extremely common in cities and towns, often open 24/7. Many medications are available without prescription, including antibiotics. Prescription rules: Many medications are available OTC. For prescription drugs, a Vietnamese doctor's prescription may be required. International prescriptions are generally not accepted. 💡 Tips Vietnam has very easy pharmacy access — many medications available OTC that require prescriptions elsewhere, including antibiotics. However, quality of medications can be inconsistent. Buy from reputable pharmacies (large chains like Long Chau, Pharmacity, or Nexus) when possible. Recommended vaccinations: Hepatitis A, Hepatitis B, Typhoid, Japanese Encephalitis (for rural stays), Rabies (for animal contact), COVID-19 (following current guidelines). Malaria risk is present — consult a travel doctor before visiting. Public hospitals require payment upfront. Medical evacuation from rural areas to Bangkok or Singapore may be necessary for serious conditions.
